t: LeetCode 3214 – Year on Year Growth Rate (SQL)
o: Aggregate spend per (product, year), then for each year attach the previous year's total and compute the percentage growth rounded to 2 decimals; the earliest year per product gets NULLs. Window function LAG over (product_id ORDER BY year) does this in one pass. In the example, 2020 shows (1000.20 − 1500.60)/1500.60 = −33.35%.
k: LAG(spend) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY year) fetches the prior-year total.
Guard division against NULL/zero and ROUND to 2 places.

a.i: First CTE reduces transactions to yearly totals; second CTE computes LAG once; the outer select formats the growth rate so the NULL first year falls out naturally.
s: Group by YEAR(transaction_date), product_id and sum spend.
Apply LAG partitioned by product, ordered by year.
Compute ROUND((curr - prev)/prev * 100, 2) and order by product_id, year.

c.python:
WITH yearly AS (
    SELECT YEAR(transaction_date) AS yr,
           product_id,
           SUM(spend) AS s
    FROM user_transactions
    GROUP BY yr, product_id
),
lagged AS (
    SELECT yr, product_id, s,
           LAG(s) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY yr) AS prev_s
    FROM yearly
)
SELECT yr AS year,
       product_id,
       s AS curr_year_spend,
       prev_s AS prev_year_spend,
       ROUND((s - prev_s) / prev_s * 100, 2) AS yoy_rate
FROM lagged
ORDER BY product_id, yr;

a.i: Join the yearly totals to themselves matching each (product, year) with (product, year − 1); a LEFT JOIN preserves the first year with a NULL previous spend.
s: Aggregate to yearly totals in a CTE.
LEFT JOIN the CTE to itself on product_id and a.yr = b.yr + 1.
Compute the rounded rate (NULL-safe) and order.

c.python:
WITH yearly AS (
    SELECT YEAR(transaction_date) AS yr,
           product_id,
           SUM(spend) AS s
    FROM user_transactions
    GROUP BY yr, product_id
)
SELECT a.yr AS year,
       a.product_id,
       a.s AS curr_year_spend,
       b.s AS prev_year_spend,
       ROUND((a.s - b.s) / b.s * 100, 2) AS yoy_rate
FROM yearly a
LEFT JOIN yearly b
    ON a.product_id = b.product_id AND a.yr = b.yr + 1
ORDER BY a.product_id, a.yr;

w: All code blocks contain the same MySQL statement — the problem is purely SQL. Prefer LAG: it is declarative and handles gaps in years consistently (LAG takes the previous available row; a strict calendar-year comparison would need the self-join with yr = yr − 1, which yields NULL for missing years). Pitfalls: dividing by zero/NULL, forgetting ROUND(...,2), and aliasing the reserved word year. Follow-up: quarter-over-quarter growth, or products with missing intermediate years.
